author: EmuCore - Hub
title: Primal: using Jen and Scree to connect four demon realms without abandoning companion character
summary: Cambridge Studio paired Jen's evolving demon forms with Scree's climbing and possession abilities, using an AI companion and realm-specific production to sustain a long cinematic action adventure.

blocks.text: Jen handles combat and gains forms suited to different realms, while Scree climbs stone surfaces, squeezes through routes and can animate statues. Switching changes what architecture means. A wall ignored by Jen may be a path for Scree; a hostile encounter manageable by Jen may be avoided while the companion searches for another solution.
The inactive partner must remain believable

When the player controls one character, the other follows, waits or reacts through AI. Companion pathfinding has to cope with traversal changes and camera transitions without constantly becoming the objective. The design also uses dialogue during movement, allowing the relationship to develop outside cutscenes while reassuring the player that Scree or Jen remains present.

Jen's transformations are tied to realms and provide more than cosmetic armor. Movement, combat rhythm and energy use change, making progression a collection of embodied solutions. The human protagonist remains recognizable through voice and intention, so transformation expands her agency without replacing her with unrelated selectable characters.

Solum, Aquis, Aetha and Volca use different architecture, inhabitants, lighting and elemental logic. The hub-like Nexus connects them into one cosmology. This variety gives the long adventure visual chapters, but it increases production cost because enemies, effects and traversal assumptions cannot be reused invisibly across every environment.
Scree makes stone an active resource

The gargoyle can climb, collect energy and inhabit statues, turning decorative masonry into traversal and puzzle machinery. His smaller body and different camera height change spatial reading. Because he is also a speaking companion, mechanical utility and characterization share one presence rather than splitting into tool icons and exposition voice.

Extended dialogue, facial performance and authored camera work aim for a television-drama scale. These strengths can slow repeated traversal when interaction density falls. Primal illustrates the PS2 era's push toward long-form cinematic adventures before streaming worlds and companion AI were fully routine, including the friction between spectacle and immediate control.

Blocks, attacks and finishers depend on readable enemy animation and Jen's current capabilities. The system is less expressive than specialist character-action games, but it supports narrative transformation. Encounters teach when a form's power is appropriate and make energy management part of surviving a realm, rather than allowing permanent unrestricted demon strength.

QA must switch characters across climbs, doors, combat and realm transitions, checking that the inactive partner teleports or catches up only as intended. Audio streaming and dialogue sync are central to tone. Widescreen changes can expose off-camera companion repositioning, while frame-rate patches may disturb combat and scripted environmental timing.
Why the partnership carries the game

Primal's realms are memorable, but Jen and Scree give them continuity. Their contrasting bodies let one environment support different traversal, and their conversation prevents mechanical switching from feeling like a menu abstraction. The production succeeds when a technical companion requirement becomes a relationship the player wants to preserve across a very long journey.
